passage_text: Researchers at the University of Greenfield investigated the effect of a novel probiotic on weight gain in laboratory mice. A total of 80 mice were randomly assigned to either a control group (n = 40) receiving a standard diet or a treatment group (n = 40) receiving the same diet supplemented with the probiotic. The study spanned 28 days, with body weights recorded weekly. At the end of the study, the mean body weight of the control group was 30.2 g (SD = 1.5 g), whereas the treatment group averaged 32.8 g (SD = 1.3 g). A two‑tailed t‑test yielded a p‑value < 0.001, indicating a statistically significant difference between groups. The researchers also measured serum short‑chain fatty acids (SCFAs) and found higher acetate levels in the treatment group, suggesting a potential mechanistic link. The study concluded that probiotic supplementation may promote modest weight gain in mice, possibly mediated by altered gut microbiota metabolism.
stem: What was the percent increase in mean body weight of the treatment group compared to the control group at the end of the study?
trap: Option B divides by the treatment mean (2.6/32.8 ≈ 7.9%); the control mean is the correct reference.

stem: Which experimental design feature best ensures that the observed weight difference is attributable to the probiotic?

options.A: Using a larger sample size than required
options.B: Random assignment of mice to groups
options.D: Conducting a t‑test at the study’s end

explanation: Random assignment controls for confounding variables, making it more likely that the probiotic is the cause of the weight difference.
trap: Option C is tempting because frequent measurement improves data quality, but it does not directly control for confounding factors.

stem: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by the study data?

options.A: Treatment-group mean weight was higher than control-group mean weight at every weekly measurement after day 0.
options.B: The between-group difference in mean weight was larger at day 28 than at day 0.
options.C: Acetate levels were higher in the treatment group.
options.D: The higher acetate levels were shown to cause the weight difference.

explanation: Correct: D. Acetate was only measured and found higher in the treatment group; no experiment manipulated acetate, so causation is not shown (the passage says only a potential link). Why the others are wrong: A) The treatment means (29.5, 30.5, 31.5, 32.8) exceed the control means (29, 29.5, 30, 30.2) at days 7 to 28, so A is supported. B) The difference was 0.1 g at day 0 and 2.6 g at day 28, so B is supported. C) The passage reports higher acetate in the treatment group, so C is supported.
trap: Reading an observed association between acetate and weight as proof of cause.

stem: The study measured serum short‑chain fatty acids such as acetate. Which statement about these molecules is correct?

options.A: They are produced by bacterial fermentation of otherwise indigestible dietary fiber and can be absorbed by the host as an additional energy source.
options.B: They are synthesized by pancreatic lipase from dietary triglycerides.
options.C: They are made only by host colonocytes and not by gut bacteria.
options.D: They cannot cross the colonic epithelium and are excreted unchanged.

explanation: Gut anaerobes ferment non-digestible fiber into short-chain fatty acids (acetate, propionate, butyrate), which colonocytes and the host absorb and use for energy. This provides a plausible link between altered microbiota metabolism and increased weight gain.
trap: Option B confuses SCFAs with free fatty acids released by lipase; SCFAs are products of bacterial fermentation.
